newsitem.title: USA: Fugitive prosecutor featured on TV crime show.
newsitem.headline: Fugitive prosecutor featured on TV crime show.

text.p: A former New Jersey county prosecutor will have the dubious distinction of twice having appeared on the television show "America's Most Wanted" -- first as a law enforcement agent and now as a fugitive, a show spokeswoman said Monday.
Former Somerset County prosecutor Nicholas Bissell has been the subject of a nationwide manhunt since he disappeared last week days before he was to be sentenced on federal criminal charges.
Bissell snipped his electronic monitoring bracelet and left a suicide note before vanishing from his Franklin Township, New Jersey, home Nov. 18, but authorities doubted its validity.

His story will appear on the popular Fox Network show this Saturday, said "America's Most Wanted" spokeswoman Kathy Swanda. Last year Bissell appeared on the show as a prosecutor in an unrelated case of jewel theft, Swanda said.
"We have never before had a subject who was first featured as a law enforcement officer and then as a criminal," she said.

Bissell was scheduled to be sentenced last Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Newark, New Jersey, on 30 federal charges, including fraud and tax evasion. He had been free under home confinement on $300,000 bail.
Also on Monday, the local police union, an old nemesis of Bissell's, offered a $1,000 reward for his capture.
"To know Nicholas Bissell was to dislike him," said Mike Gilhooly, president of the Franklin Township Policemen's Benevolent Association, who called Bissell arrogant.

"This is get-even time for us," he said, recalling an incident in 1991 when Bissell tried to seize control of the township's detective bureau after objecting to its use of a police dog in a burglary case.
Bissell was appointed county prosecutor in 1982 and dismissed last year after he was indicted.

He was accused of skimming $146,000 from receipts of a gasoline filling station he and his wife partly owned to support a lavish lifestyle of fancy cars, expensive jewelry and hefty credit card charges.

Bissell also was convicted of professional corruption, misconduct and abuse of power, including ordering the destruction of a suspect's written request for an attorney, lying on ethics disclosure forms and lying to investigators.
He faced a minimum of six-and-a half to 10 years in prison. A jury convicted Bissell of 30 charges and his wife Barbara on 13 charges in late May.
